entries.title: The 89 best REI Labor Day deals, from a $16 sock to a $1,499-off e-bike
entries.content:
REI runs two big sales a year and the Labor Day event is where the co-op clears summer stock before winter inventory needs the shelf space. That means tents, sleeping pads, camp chairs, and trail shoes get cut hardest just in time to enjoy the tail end of warm weather. The [Labor Day sale](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Ff%2Fscd-deals&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) runs through September 7, and REI members who spend $50 or more also earn a $30 single-use promo card during the same window. I went through roughly 2,500 discounted items and pulled the size runs on every pair of shoes below, because a 50 percent markdown on a shoe that only exists in a men’s 9.5 isn’t a deal, it’s a leftover.

### NEMO Stargaze Evo-X Folding Reclining Camp Chair $99.99 (was $179.95)

A suspended, rocking camp chair for $80 off, in five colors

[![Nemo Stargaze Evo-X Folding Reclining Camp Chair](https://www.popsci.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/nemo-.jpg?quality=85&w=768)

Nem](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F242354%2Fnemo-stargaze-evo-x-folding-reclining-camp-chair&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699)

[See It](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F242354%2Fnemo-stargaze-evo-x-folding-reclining-camp-chair&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699)

The [NEMO Stargaze Evo-X](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F242354%2Fnemo-stargaze-evo-x-folding-reclining-camp-chair&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) at $99.99 hangs the seat from a frame so the whole chair swings and reclines without you doing anything, which is a different experience from sitting in a folding quad chair, and it usually costs $179.95. All five colorways are live at this price. NEMO rates it to 300 pounds and it packs into its own carry bag.

### HOKA Clifton 10 Road-Running Shoes $99.83 (was $155.00)

The current Clifton, not last year’s model, under $100 in both men’s and women’s

[![Hoke Clifton sneaker on grass](https://www.popsci.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/hoka-clifton-rei-sale.jpg?quality=85&w=768)

Hoka](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F242661%2Fhoka-clifton-10-road-running-shoes-mens&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699)

[See It](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F242661%2Fhoka-clifton-10-road-running-shoes-mens&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699)

You won’t typically find current-generation [HOKA Clifton 10](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F242661%2Fhoka-clifton-10-road-running-shoes-mens&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) under $100 while it’s still the model on the store shelves. The men’s version has 30 sizes live and the [women’s Clifton 10](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F242759%2Fhoka-clifton-10-road-running-shoes-womens&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) has 34, so this is a real size run rather than a picked-over one. Both are $99.83, down from $155.

### Hydro Flask Wide-Mouth 32 fl. oz. Water Bottle with Flex Cap $30.73 (was $44.95)

The standard 32-ounce Hydro Flask, in the two colors REI marked down

[![Purple Hydro Flask water bottle on grass](https://www.popsci.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/hydro-flask-water-bottle-rei-deal.jpg?quality=85&w=768)

Hydro Flask](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F207804%2Fhydro-flask-wide-mouth-vacuum-water-bottle-with-flex-cap-32-fl-oz&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699)

[See It](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F207804%2Fhydro-flask-wide-mouth-vacuum-water-bottle-with-flex-cap-32-fl-oz&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699)

Hydro Flask discounts are usually colorway-specific, and this one is no exception. The [32-ounce Wide-Mouth with the Flex Cap](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F207804%2Fhydro-flask-wide-mouth-vacuum-water-bottle-with-flex-cap-32-fl-oz&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) is $30.73 instead of $44.95, but only two colors are still live at that price, so pick before you deliberate. This is the plain vacuum-insulated bottle with the loop lid, not a straw or tumbler variant.

### Garmin inReach Messenger $199.99 (was $300.00)

Two-way satellite texting and SOS for $100 off

[![Garmin Inreach messenger on grass](https://www.popsci.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/garmin-inreach-messenger-rei.jpg?quality=85&w=768)

Garmin](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F216799%2Fgarmin-inreach-messenger&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699)

[See It](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F216799%2Fgarmin-inreach-messenger&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699)

The [Garmin inReach Messenger](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F216799%2Fgarmin-inreach-messenger&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) is my wife’s go-to choice when venturing into a world without cellphone reception. It’s the stripped-down inReach, so you get two-way messaging, location sharing, and an SOS button routed to Garmin’s response center, without the maps and navigation of a Mini 2. Garmin rates the battery at up to 28 days in 10-minute tracking mode. A satellite subscription is required and sold separately, which is the part people forget to budget for.

### Mountain Hardwear Mineral King 3 Tent with Footprint $239.99 (was $400.00)

A three-person tent with the footprint already in the box, $160 off

[![Mountain Hard Wear Mineral King 3 Tent with Footprint](https://www.popsci.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/mountain-hard-wear-.jpg?quality=85&w=768)

Mountain Hard Wear](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F244686%2Fmountain-hardwear-mineral-king-3-tent-with-footprint&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699)

[See It](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F244686%2Fmountain-hardwear-mineral-king-3-tent-with-footprint&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699)

Tent footprints are the accessory everyone skips and then buys separately at full price, so the [Mountain Hardwear Mineral King 3](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F244686%2Fmountain-hardwear-mineral-king-3-tent-with-footprint&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) including one at $239.99 does better than the $160 off suggests. It’s a freestanding three-person with two doors and two vestibules, which is the layout worth paying for if two people plus gear is the actual load. The [two-person version](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F244542%2Fmountain-hardwear-mineral-king-2-tent-with-footprint&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) is $209.99 if you never carry a third body.

## Best REI Labor Day tent deals

Tents are the deepest cut in this sale. The [Mountain Hardwear Mineral King 2](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F244542%2Fmountain-hardwear-mineral-king-2-tent-with-footprint&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) at $209.99 is 40 percent off with the footprint in the box, and the [Coleman Skydome 4-Person](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F246471%2Fcoleman-skydome-4-person-tent-with-full-fly-vestibule&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) at $142.49 is the least expensive tent here that sleeps four under a full rain fly.

* [**Coleman Skydome 4-Person Tent with Full-Fly Vestibule**](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F246471%2Fcoleman-skydome-4-person-tent-with-full-fly-vestibule&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) $142.49 (was $190.00)
* [**Marmot Tungsten 2P Tent with Footprint**](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F200288%2Fmarmot-tungsten-2p-tent-with-footprint&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) $208.93 (was $279.00)
* [**Marmot Limelight 3-Person Tent with Footprint**](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2FC12183%2Fmarmot-limelight-3-person-tent-with-footprint&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) $274.87 (was $399.00)
* [**Mountain Hardwear Nimbus UL 2 Tent**](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F244544%2Fmountain-hardwear-nimbus-ul-2-tent&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) $344.99 (was $460.00)
* [**Gazelle T4 Hub Tent**](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F207747%2Fgazelle-t4-hub-tent&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) $377.93 (was $539.95)
* [**Big Agnes Tiger Wall UL3 Bikepack Solution Dye Tent**](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2FC07269%2Fbig-agnes-tiger-wall-ul3-bikepack-solution-dye-tent&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) $383.87 (was $549.95)

## Best sleeping bag and sleeping pad deals from $37

Sleeping pads discount more reliably than bags do, and this year is no different. The [Therm-a-Rest Z Lite Sol](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F171690%2Ftherm-a-rest-z-lite-sol-sleeping-pad&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) starts at $37.39, and the [REI Co-op Magma 15](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F228704%2Frei-co-op-magma-15-sleeping-bag&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) starting at $299.19 is the least expensive 15-degree down bag I turned up in the sale.

* [**Therm-a-Rest Z Lite Sol Sleeping Pad**](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F171690%2Ftherm-a-rest-z-lite-sol-sleeping-pad&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) $37.39-$44.89 (was $49.95-$59.95)
* [**Sea to Summit Aeros Premium Pillow**](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2FC04276%2Fsea-to-summit-aeros-premium-pillow&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) $41.19-$52.39 (was $54.95-$69.95)
* [**Therm-a-Rest NeoAir XLite NXT MAX Sleeping Pad**](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F241035%2Ftherm-a-rest-neoair-xlite-nxt-max-sleeping-pad&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) $164.89-$179.89 (was $219.95-$239.95)
* [**NEMO Tensor All-Season Ultralight Insulated Sleeping Pad**](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F228436%2Fnemo-tensor-all-season-ultralight-insulated-sleeping-pad&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) $164.89-$194.89 (was $219.95-$259.95)
* [**Sea to Summit Spark 45F Down Sleeping Bag**](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F231219%2Fsea-to-summit-spark-45f-down-sleeping-bag&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) $261.69 (was $349.00)
* [**REI Co-op Magma 15 Sleeping Bag**](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F228704%2Frei-co-op-magma-15-sleeping-bag&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) $299.19-$314.19 (was $399.00-$419.00)
* [**Exped MegaMat Duo Sleeping Pad**](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F238244%2Fexped-megamat-duo-sleeping-pad&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) $299.89-$412.39 (was $399.95-$549.95)

## Best camp stove, coffee, and water filter deals under $125

This is the section where the prices are low enough that you buy the thing you’ve been meaning to replace. The [MSR PocketRocket 2](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F114890%2Fmsr-pocketrocket-2-stove&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) at $44.89 is the canister stove I’d hand a first-time backpacker, and the [Platypus QuickDraw](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F232555%2Fplatypus-quickdraw-filter&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) at $29.89 is the cheapest hollow-fiber filter here.

* [**Platypus QuickDraw Filter**](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F232555%2Fplatypus-quickdraw-filter&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) $29.89 (was $39.95)
* [**LifeStraw Peak Squeeze Water Filter System, 33.8 fl. oz.**](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F204127%2Flifestraw-peak-squeeze-water-filter-system-338-fl-oz&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) $32.89 (was $43.95)
* [**AeroPress Go Travel Coffee Press**](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F173365%2Faeropress-go-travel-coffee-press&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) $34.89 (was $49.95)
* [**MSR PocketRocket 2 Stove**](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F114890%2Fmsr-pocketrocket-2-stove&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) $44.89 (was $59.95)
* [**Katadyn Gravity BeFree Water Filtration System, 3 Liters**](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F139666%2Fkatadyn-gravity-befree-water-filtration-system-3-liters&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) $59.89 (was $79.95)
* [**Jetboil Stash Cooking System**](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F186174%2Fjetboil-stash-cooking-system&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) $123.69 (was $164.95)

## Best camp chair, cooler, and camp furniture deals

Camp furniture is the category people wait on sales for, and the [Coleman Broadband Mesh Quad Chair](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F218132%2Fcoleman-broadband-mesh-quad-chair&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) at $26.59 is the cheap one that will outlast three seasons of tailgates. The [Rumpl Backcountry Puffy Blanket](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F237296%2Frumpl-backcountry-puffy-blanket&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) at $89.83 is the one I’d add if you already own chairs.

* [**Coleman Broadband Mesh Quad Chair**](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F218132%2Fcoleman-broadband-mesh-quad-chair&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) $26.59 (was $35.50)
* [**REI Co-op Campwell 18 L Folding Cooler**](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F245796%2Frei-co-op-campwell-18-l-folding-cooler&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) $27.93-$29.89 (was $39.95)
* [**REI Co-op Camp Low Chair**](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F242895%2Frei-co-op-camp-low-chair&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) $52.39 (was $69.95)
* [**REI Co-op Flexlite Camp Chair**](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F228236%2Frei-co-op-flexlite-camp-chair&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) $67.39 (was $89.95)
* [**Rumpl Backcountry Puffy Blanket**](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F237296%2Frumpl-backcountry-puffy-blanket&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) $89.89 (was $149.95)
* [**Big Agnes Big Six Camp Chair**](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F231931%2Fbig-agnes-big-six-camp-chair&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) $186.93 (was $249.95)

## Best hiking boot and hiking shoe deals

Hiking footwear held its size runs better than road shoes did here. The [Merrell Moab 3](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F232969%2Fmerrell-moab-3-hiking-shoes-mens&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) at $104.73 is the default recommendation for a reason and it’s discounted in both men’s and women’s, while the [Arc’teryx Kopec Mid GTX](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F235366%2Farcteryx-kopec-mid-gtx-hiking-boots-mens&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) at $139.93 is the closest thing to a bargain Arc’teryx ever gets.

* [**Merrell Moab 3 Hiking Shoes, Men’s**](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F232969%2Fmerrell-moab-3-hiking-shoes-mens&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) $104.73 (was $140.00)
* [**Merrell Moab 3 Hiking Shoes, Women’s**](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F233039%2Fmerrell-moab-3-hiking-shoes-womens&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) $104.73 (was $120.00-$140.00)
* [**Salomon Elixir Activ Mid GORE-TEX Hiking Boots, Men’s**](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F236023%2Fsalomon-elixir-activ-mid-gore-tex-hiking-boots-mens&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) $118.93 (was $170.00)
* [**KEEN Hightrail Mid Waterproof Hiking Boots, Men’s**](https://rei.pxf.io/c/6430275/1448521/17195?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rei.com%2Fproduct%2F246731%2Fkeen-hightrail-mid-waterproof-hiking-boots-mens&partnerpropertyid=7325699&MediaPartnerPropertyId=7325699) $119.99 (was $160.00)

entries.title: I Ditched My Bone-Conduction Headphones for These Noise-Cancelling Running Earbuds
entries.content:
We may earn a commission from links on this page.

Running earbuds are an extremely personal [category of gear](https://lifehacker.com/health/best-headphones-earbuds-for-running). Every runner has their own non-negotiables. For me, the top priority has always been a secure fit—which is exactly why I've gravitated toward wraparound designs like the [Shokz OpenRun](https://lifehacker.com/health/shokz-openrun-air-2-review) models. I like the safety perks of open-ear, bone-conduction listening too: being able to hear traffic, cyclists, and other runners is more important than hearing my music, personally. Unfortunately, that means I've lived with a serious trade-off in sound quality. There are certain stretches of my city runs that my open-ear headphones just can't cut through. Still, every time I've tried a noise-cancelling option, I've always found some other dealbreaker with comfort, fit, or safety. So it says something that, for the first time, I actually like a pair of noise-cancelling sport earbuds: the [JLab JBuds Sport ANC 4](https://zdcs.link/9gJJ8D?pageview_type=RSS&template=content&module=content_body&element=offer&item=text-link&element_label=JLab%20JBuds%20Sport%20ANC%204&object_type=content&short_url=9gJJ8D&u=https%3A%2F%2Flifehacker.com%2Ffeed%2Frss "open in a new window").

![JLab, JBuds Sport ANC 4, True Wireless Earbuds, Active Noise Cancelling, Bluetooth, Multipoint Connect, Cobalt Blue](https://lifehacker.com/imagery/product/05BqIhR0Zi9wyNkfJewJ4jH/hero-image.fill.size_autoxauto.v1788367725.jpg)

## Why I love these noise-cancelling sport earbuds

First things first: As far as running earbuds go, these are a budget pick at $69.99. A few other highlights:

* **60+ hours of total playtime** and **IP66 sweat resistance**
* **Flexible over-the-ear hooks** for a secure fit
* A **well-designed charging case** with a built-in USB-C cable *and* wireless charging support (the one catch: the built-in cable is short, so the case needs to stay close to an outlet)

I tested these on the Williamsburg Bridge—one of the loudest, windiest stretches in my regular rotation, and a place where my go-to open-ear pair, the [Shokz OpenRun Pro 2](https://lifehacker.com/tech/review-shokz-openrun-pro-2-bone-conduction-headphones), simply get drowned out. The JBuds Sport ANC 4 handled it admirably. I could actually hear my music along with the foot traffic around me, all without losing the secure fit I need to trust earbuds on a run.

I'm over 30 miles into testing them now, and they haven't shifted once. Fit is always subjective—what locks in for my ears might not work for yours—but this is the first ANC sport earbud that's matched what I get from a wraparound design.

If touch controls are an important consideration for you, JLab did something interesting here: there are two separate touch surfaces, one on the outer shell and one on the hook itself, which supports swipe gestures. Out of the box, the controls are the same for both ears:

* **Single tap:** play/pause
* **Double tap:** next track
* **Triple tap:** previous track
* **Long press:** cycle through Noise Cancelling, Be Aware (transparency), and Off
* **Swipe:** volume control

Everything is customizable in the app, including setting independent controls per earbud. You can reassign gestures to switch EQ presets, trigger your voice assistant, or control the workout timer.

The "Be Aware" mode (JLab's transparency setting) is fine for quick in-person conversations, but it's not great. It amplifies most ambient sound but struggles with higher frequencies and introduces a noticeable hiss, which makes voices and traffic sound a bit synthetic.

And to be clear: this is an upgrade for **running earbuds**, not a hi-fi listening upgrade. If premium sound quality is your top priority, look elsewhere.

## The bottom line

I wouldn't recommend these to everyone. If pristine sound is what you're after, this isn't your pair. But if you're coming from an open-ear or bone-conduction setup like Shokz and you've hit the same wall I have—where city noise simply overwhelms the open design—then JBuds Sport ANC 4 hits a specific, useful sweet spot. For me, these have enough noise cancellation to make loud routes bearable, a fit secure enough to trust through a hard workout, and a budget price.

entries.title: NYC Public Schools Ban AI Use Through Middle School
entries.content:
New York City Public Schools is banning generative AI for students from pre-K through eighth grade for the 2026-27 school year, affecting more than half a million students in the nation's largest school district. ABC News reports: In a statement to ABC News, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said that the city is implementing a moratorium on generative AI for students in pre-school or 2-K through eighth grade and will spend the next year "studying the impacts of this technology." Mamdani wrote in part, "the tech industry wants us to believe that A.I.-powered early education is not only inevitable, but necessary." "We do not see it that way," he added.
[...] The district said it is implementing the most expansive AI moratorium in the nation, eliminating software that uses student-facing AI and banning companion chatbots. The city's AI moratorium does not apply to high school students. The district said it will offer twice-yearly AI literacy classes designed to help high school students "think critically" about the technology before they start to "rely" on it.

[![](https://a.fsdn.com/sd/twitter_icon_large.png)](http://twitter.com/home?status=NYC+Public+Schools+Ban+AI+Use+Through+Middle+School%3A+https%3A%2F%2Fnews.slashdot.org%2Fstory%2F26%2F09%2F02%2F167206%2F%3Futm_source%3Dtwitter%26utm_medium%3Dtwitter)
[![](https://a.fsdn.com/sd/facebook_icon_large.png)](http://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fnews.slashdot.org%2Fstory%2F26%2F09%2F02%2F167206%2Fnyc-public-schools-ban-ai-use-through-middle-school%3Futm_source%3Dslashdot%26utm_medium%3Dfacebook)

entries.title: Enterprise-managed settings support any default model
entries.content:
![The managed.json file showing an update to the default model where the current model key is replaced with "Kimi 3"](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/70173fe2-94ea-442e-a1f4-04e35e366b41)  
You can now set your preferred GitHub Copilot model as the default for new conversations through enterprise-managed settings. This lets you choose the default model that best fits your workflows.

You can also customize the default by enterprise team, assigning a different default model based on team membership. Set the `model` key as `overridable` and update team configuration files in `team-mappings.json` so that enterprise teams can choose their own preferred default model. All other users inherit your enterprise default. Model defaults in managed settings are generally available with Copilot Business and Copilot Enterprise in the GitHub Copilot app, Copilot CLI, and Visual Studio Code.

Learn more in [our docs about enterprise managed settings](https://docs.github.com/enterprise-cloud@latest/copilot/reference/enterprise-administrators/enterprise-managed-settings#model), or join the discussion in the [GitHub Community](https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/199139).

The post [Enterprise-managed settings support any default model](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-09-02-enterprise-managed-settings-support-any-default-model) appeared first on [The GitHub Blog](https://github.blog).

entries.content:
基本上你只要让 Fable 指挥其他 Agent 干活，这两个进度条就能持平。  
  
大部分任务你选 Fable + High（或者Medium，千万别Max及以上），然后后面加一句：  
> 注意你的主要任务是分析、编排和验证，具体任务尽可能交给 subagent（Opus 或 Sonnet）去执行。自己只做需求澄清、方案拆解、任务分发和结果验收，实现类工作（读大量代码、写代码、跑测试、批量修改）一律用 Agent 工具派给 subagent 执行。

![WquGuru](https://pbs.twimg.com/profile_images/1892575619298525184/q8syuBou_normal.jpg)

WquGuru@wquguru

另一个 Claude Code token 管理技巧：看 /usage 时，把周度总消耗和 Fable 周度消耗两条进度条尽量对齐。  
  
Fable 更贵、更聪明，但是额度只有总额度的 50%，很容易出现两种失衡：  
  
Fable 条已经 70%，总用量才 40%，智力额度见底，后面只能强行降智  
总用量 70%，Fable 才 20%，便宜模型烧得太猛，最强模型的窗口反而被浪费了  
  
对齐也不必机械对半，找一个自己感觉比较良好的比例，而是让周额度和Fable额度大致成比例下降即可，一些性价比高的落地做法：  
  
主会话用 Fable 做判断、架构、拆任务、复盘；执行、检索、改文件、跑测试丢给 Opus 子代理。  
  
任务切换就 /clear，长任务中途 /compact。  
  
每天看几次进度条，Fable 超前就减少 Fable 使用强度；总进度条超前就多把一些关键决策交回 Fable。  
  
实测下来，这种节奏能让智力密度和额度一起走到重置日，达到一个最佳的状态。

entries.title: Gemini 3.8 Flash (High) by @GoogleDeepMind significantly improved in Agent Arena over Gemini 3.7 Fla...
entries.content:
Gemini 3.8 Flash (High) by [@GoogleDeepMind](https://x.com/GoogleDeepMind) significantly improved in Agent Arena over Gemini 3.7 Flash (High), scoring +5.94% net improvement and ranking #14 overall—up from +0.84% and #32 overall for 3.7!  
  
Agent Arena measures net improvement relative to the average model across real-world, long-horizon tasks using web, filesystem, and terminal tools. We measure overall and dive deeper by five key signals:  
  
- Confirmed Success: explicit “yes, that worked” from users  
- Praise vs. Complaint: implicit sentiment in users reactions  
- Steerability: can the model course-correct when you push back?  
- Bash Recovery: how it recovers from CLI errors  
- Tool Hallucination: does it call tools that don't exist  
  
Of the five key signals we track, Gemini 3.8 Flash (High) demonstrates a massive gain in Praise vs. Complaint: users are reacting to its output with noticeably more positive sentiment. There is notable improvement in Confirmed Success, and Bash Recovery. Steerability remains a relative weakness, though it has improved compared with 3.7.  
  
Gemini 3.8 Flash (High) vs. Gemini 3.7 Flash (High):  
- Praise vs. Complaint: +14.78% vs -1.60%  
- Confirmed Success: +11.12% vs +9.80%  
- Bash Recovery: +4.46% vs +0.61%  
- Steerability: -1.43% vs -5.38%  
- Tool Hallucination: Scores were nearly identical, with neither model showing issues  
  
Big congrats to the [@GoogleDeepMind](https://x.com/GoogleDeepMind) team on this release!

entries.title: From MIT to IBM, expediting AI and quantum deployment
entries.content:
The experience of transitioning from research based in theory to focusing on real-world application can vary significantly for different researchers. However, for two former MIT graduate students and a former postdoc, all now at IBM, working with the MIT-IBM Computing Research Lab (formerly the MIT-IBM Watson AI Lab) during their formative years enabled them to not only close the gap between education and employment, but also to generate ideas promising to business impact.

Despite pursuing varied careers in quantum machine learning, reinforcement learning and artificial intelligence agents,and trustworthy and fair AI, respectively, [Srinivasan Arunachalam](https://logitechenator.github.io/sarunach/), [Zhang-Wei Hong](https://williamd4112.github.io/) PhD ’25, and [Irene Ko](https://ireneko.github.io/) PhD ’24 have consistently found ways to tackle problems defined by novelty and rigor, and translate them to systems with real constraints. Here, the MIT-IBM Computing Research Lab served as a conduit for research relationship building and the flow of their expertise to industry applications.

“Among all the industrial labs, I think MIT-IBM has way better academic collaboration policy and opportunity [than the others],” says Hong, an IBM research staff member with the MIT-IBM Computing Research Lab who began his PhD at MIT in 2020 in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS).

Hong has been captivated with reinforcement learning since discovering that DeepMind could play Atari and learn from raw screen pixels via feature engineering. During his graduate work with EECS Associate Professor Pulkit Agrawal, who is also a principal investigator with the lab, Hong sought to build on this: improving value function learning for reinforcement learning in video games, using “Montezuma’s Revenge” in Atari, in order to predict and optimize the policy performance of an agent. With the lab, Hong developed techniques to ground AI for more realistic applications and provide better reward feedback, which he applied to domains such as robotics, large language models (LLMs), and reinforcement learning for science.

“I’m very excited about curiosity-driven exploration,” says Hong of the MIT-IBM graduate work that helped propel him into his profession. This, he says, allows agents to be inquisitive about new data, like humans, and perform a variety of tasks — from generating test cases to stress-test LLMs to exploring new environments. Now, as a mentor for students of his own, Hong continues to pursue similar lines of open-ended reinforcement learning research, leading him to investigate test-time training for agents and foundation models, and develop infrastructure for IBM’s agentic framework for enterprise tasks like chart reading and tool calling for database queries. This includes evolutionary computing to drive better optimization for exploration and leveraging neuroscience to inform deployment time model improvement.

“If successful, I think that it would be a very useful system and framework for all of the practitioners in reinforcement learning, because it will be the first framework that enables a model to improve — self-evolve their model weights online at a deployment time,” says Hong.

Irene Ko’s research has also been value-driven, from a personal and professional standpoint. “I started to work [on trustworthy AI] with IBM researchers from day 1 in my PhD, because it was funded by MIT-IBM,” says Ko. This, she says, was particularly advantageous since her goals to develop frontier-safe, robust, accurate, and fair AI also align with that of MIT and IBM, closing the gap between development and real-world deployment. “That really strikes a balance between pure research and something that’s of industry standard or value.”

Further, her MIT-IBM collaboration through her advisor in EECS, Joseph F. and Nancy P. Keithley Professor Luca Daniel, and IBM Principal Research Scientist Pin-Yu Chen, helped define the direction and parameters of her work to maximize impact, first in neural networks and later with foundation models and LLMs. After graduating in 2024, Ko joined IBM Research to continue her work on trustworthy AI as a research scientist.

“The reason I chose to go into industry after my PhD, and IBM specifically, is that I found great joy in the collaboration during my PhD. That process, those five years, gave me very high rewards in personal fulfillment,” says Ko. “I wanted to continue the momentum.”

Her current project focuses on finding pain points in current trustworthy methods that are not widely deployed in AI inference platforms. Unlike using low-rank adapters, which add extra steps to monitor and modify model behavior, her work on [vLLM Hook](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.06588) provides a way to access internal model signals, like hidden states or activations, for decoding LLMs. This vector acts on transformer modules to analyze safety scores, such as identifying the likelihood of prompt-injection and hallucination. Here, Ko has developed a lightweight vLLM inference engine plugin framework to program the model internals that could provide significant cost savings over other methods. “I’m very proud of this project because this is really, as far as we know, the first bridge between the deployment and development in trustworthy AI with the inference engines.”

While SrinivasanArunachalam has always dabbled in quantum research, he constantly explores other areas of theory, seeking to find quantum insights and deep math in unexpected lines of inquiry and papers. “Right off the bat, you don’t see it. You think, maybe this is just a vanilla problem, and then once you start investigating it further, you find some really interesting math that comes out of it, which I think is pretty cool,” he says.

This drew Arunachalam to MIT as a postdoc in 2018 in the group of Professor Aram Harrow in the Department of Physics. With a learning theory-first perspective, Arunachalam looked for target algorithms, subroutines, and circuits where quantum speed-ups might be possible. Conversations with Isaac Chuang, the Julius A. Stratton Professor in Electrical Engineering and Physics and an MIT-IBM PI, led him to collaborate with the lab and IBM researcher Kristan Temme.

With a seamless transition to IBM, Arunachalam more closely involved himself with problems that are potentially implementable on a near-term quantum device, keeping in mind constraints like nearest-neighbor architecture, noise, and simpler observable measurements. During this time, Arunachalam focused on quantum machine learning and areas where quantum computing would be superior to classical computing, increasingly prioritizing provability grounded in theory to heuristics. That MIT-IBM connection helped turn theoretical questions into concrete research directions, shaping work that culminated in two prominent papers: one on [Hamiltonian learning](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41567-021-01232-0), which gave rigorous guarantees for learning the dynamics of quantum systems, and another on [quantum kernels](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41567-021-01287-z "https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__www.nature.com_articles_s41567-2D021-2D01287-2Dz&d=DwMGaQ&c=BSDicqBQBDjDI9RkVyTcHQ&r=DnB5pyHHW7pStEbZ1xvkqcyoSlR7kH8n9uuvTBdkYW0&m=zBqVolxBrm6Ssuj7-7UtrNI7mULm3FlgsWdVfM7CsoQc4c2lm6nZ-yyrXGZeiGQE&s=2LWb"), which provided theoretical evidence that quantum feature spaces can offer advantages over classical kernels under widely believed hardness assumptions.

Arunachalam also continued to expand his knowledge base by pouring himself into different branches of computer science to uncover structure in problems others may have missed. “One thing which I’ve been a huge fan of is exposing connections between different fields.” This has allowed him to explore learning quantum states — from completely classically simulatable quantum objects to the extremely complicated quantum objects.

Although Hong, Arunachalam, and Ko navigate different domains, they share an instinct: to move ideas across the space between what is possible in principle and what is useful in practice. In their own way, each is applying knowledge gained from collaborations, like that of MIT-IBM Computing Research Lab, to develop “killer applications” — a real-world use case that proves the underlying research can matter beyond the lab.

entries.title: fix(gateway): pause clients when roles require verified identity (#13…
entries.content:
```
fix(gateway): pause clients when roles require verified identity (#136420)

Fixes #133955.

Reported by @aoclaw-glitch. Thank you for the clear trust-model and reconnect analysis.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operator clients rejected by configured Gateway role policies would reconnect forever when their auth method did not provide a verified user identity. The rejection also used broad wording and did not tell the Control UI how to recover.

## Why This Change Was Made

The handshake now returns the precise additive `AUTH_VERIFIED_USER_REQUIRED` detail and states which authentication paths work. TypeScript, Android, and Swift clients treat this outcome as terminal without clearing a valid device token. The Control UI shows verified-identity recovery steps instead of network or proxy-header troubleshooting.

The existing `AUTH_IDENTITY_HEADER_REQUIRED` code remains specific to missing trusted-proxy headers.

## User Impact

Clients stop reconnect churn after this configured-role rejection. Operators can reconnect through the trusted proxy or Tailscale, or use the shared Gateway token or password for trusted local access.

## Evidence

- Red on main `e61adf3d2c61cde99f224d590a9f0824e21ccc8e`: the real WebSocket client received the detail-less rejection twice and never paused.
- Green on head `655c283aeedeab4064234640e89b07fe5b976aa7`: the real client received `AUTH_VERIFIED_USER_REQUIRED`, made one attempt after waiting past the first reconnect delay, and retained the exact server-valid device token.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/server/ws-connection/connect-device-pairing.test.ts packages/gateway-client/src/reconnect-policy.test.ts ui/src/components/login-gate.test.ts`
- `pnpm lint:core`
- Control UI localization, formatting, max-lines, assertion-safety, coercion-helper, conflict-marker, and native-state schema guards passed.
- Local native test processes could not start because this Linux host lacks Swift and Java; pull-request CI owns native compilation and tests.

Production LOC: +39/-3 (net +36) | Tests: +127/-12

The production growth is the new cross-client error contract, terminal classifiers, and user recovery card. No configuration, persistence, or protocol version changes are included.

Provenance: PR #128548 introduced the detail-less rejection in `53dcaaedec195fdaf5af06357557c706d3c0caf5` on 2026-08-24. The raw parent is `1f1d0e9d8f2b4b05102aeb0f17ee94d06142dcac`; author and merger were @steipete.

Co-authored-by: Ayaan Zaidi <hi@obviy.us>
```

entries.title: Apple's smart home display could be coming soon, sounds amazing
entries.content:
Apple's new smart home display, designed to power [Apple Home](https://appleinsider.com/inside/apple-home "Apple Home"), could be launching soon. Here's what the rumors say will be coming, and when.  
  

![Small tablet strapped with blue tape in an X shape to a white smart speaker, screen showing a clock and controls, sitting on a gray surface with blurred background](https://media.appleinsider.com/gallery/68810-144982-Apple-Home-Display-xl.jpg)An expertly made mockup of Apple's smart home display, taping an iPad mini to a HomePod

  
A lot of what we've been hearing about this new home hub isn't exactly new. Rumors say that this device was expected to launch in the spring of 2025, before the state of [Apple Intelligence](https://appleinsider.com/inside/apple-intelligence "Apple Intelligence") forced Apple to [delay it](https://appleinsider.com/articles/26/03/09/apples-smart-home-hub-delayed-again-because-updating-siri-is-hard).  
  
But that was all in 2025, and 2026 is poised to be more promising, with Apple Intelligence and [Siri](https://appleinsider.com/inside/siri "Siri") AI on track and looking great in the recent [iOS 27](https://appleinsider.com/inside/ios-27 "iOS 27") betas. As the launch nears, we've been getting more rumors as well.  
  
  
 [Continue Reading on AppleInsider](https://appleinsider.com/articles/26/09/02/apples-smart-home-display-could-be-coming-soon-sounds-amazing?utm_source=rss) | [Discuss on our Forums](https://forums.appleinsider.com/discussion/245501?urm_source=rss)

entries.title: Wary of Artemis IV timeline, NASA is changing lunar spacesuit design
entries.content:
NASA has decided to use a simpler spacesuit for its initial missions to the lunar surface, Ars has learned.

The agency announced the decision during an internal meeting this week as it seeks to accelerate its program to land humans at the South Pole of the Moon as early as 2028. At the direction of Artemis Program Manager Jeremy Parsons, NASA will work with Axiom Space to develop a "Sortie Suit" variant of the planned spacesuit for the lunar surface.

Sources said the Sortie Suit will be used for the initial landing missions flown on landers developed both by SpaceX and Blue Origin. Among the goals of the initiative is to lower the mass of the spacesuit, reduce its complexity, and simplify interfaces between the spacesuits and lunar landers.

[Read full article](https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/09/wary-of-artemis-iv-timeline-nasa-is-changing-lunar-spacesuit-design/)

[Comments](https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/09/wary-of-artemis-iv-timeline-nasa-is-changing-lunar-spacesuit-design/#comments)
entries.summary: 为确保2028登月进度，NASA与Axiom合作开发轻量化简易登月宇航服。

entries.title: Google releases Gemini 3.8 Flash, its third Flash model in six weeks
entries.content:
Google hasn't released a frontier-level Gemini Pro AI model since early 2026, but it sure loves rolling out new Gemini Flash variants. Today, Google is [announcing its third Flash model release in just six weeks](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/3-8-flash-and-3-8-flash-cyber/), making it more likely that we'll never see the promised Gemini 3.5 Pro. But no matter, says Google, because Gemini 3.8 Flash is its best reasoning and coding model yet.

Gemini 3.8 Flash comes in two variations. There's the standard Flash, which Google describes as a "workhorse" model that's good for anything from agentic tasks to software development. Then we have Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber, which runs on the same foundations but has been tuned for vulnerability detection and mitigation.

For developers, Google has the same pitch as it did for the [3.7 Flash release](https://arstechnica.com/ai/2026/08/google-announces-gemini-3-7-flash-just-three-weeks-after-previous-release/) just a couple of weeks ago. API access to the model is available at an "introductory rate" through the end of the year: $0.75 per million input tokens and $3.75 per million output tokens. The regular price will be $1.50 / $7.50, but it's likely there will be new models available long before the price changes. Google probably sees the lower prices as a necessity given that other AI labs have recently dropped token pricing to keep increasingly wary businesses engaged with AI tools.

[Read full article](https://arstechnica.com/ai/2026/09/google-releases-gemini-3-8-flash-its-third-flash-model-in-six-weeks/)

[Comments](https://arstechnica.com/ai/2026/09/google-releases-gemini-3-8-flash-its-third-flash-model-in-six-weeks/#comments)

entries.title: Trump may be forced to reveal secret rules feds use for AI safety testing
entries.content:
Four federal agencies have been [sued](https://cdn.arstechnica.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Protect-Democracy-v-National-Cyber-Director-Complaint-9-1-26.pdf) amid calls to release information about the secret framework that the Trump administration uses to conduct [safety reviews of frontier AI models](https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2026/05/everything-that-could-go-wrong-with-trumps-ai-safety-tests-according-to-experts/) prior to release.

In a Wednesday press release announcing the lawsuit, a nonpartisan nonprofit called Protect Democracy alleged that “almost no details” have been released to the public or Congress. To everyone except a few vague “trusted partners,” it remains unclear what the government’s review process looks like, which companies are involved in constructing the framework, or what legal authority Trump officials have to conduct the reviews.

“Neither the identities of those entities nor the criteria by which they were selected have been made public,” Protect Democracy said.

[Read full article](https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2026/09/trump-may-be-forced-to-reveal-secret-rules-feds-use-for-ai-safety-testing/)

[Comments](https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2026/09/trump-may-be-forced-to-reveal-secret-rules-feds-use-for-ai-safety-testing/#comments)

entries.title: Trust is key: why home energy upgrades need more than rebates
entries.content:
![](https://images.theconversation.com/files/753491/original/file-20260812-50-nz89qq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&rect=0%2C0%2C2121%2C1414&q=45&auto=format&w=1050&h=700&fit=crop)

[AnVr/Getty](https://www.gettyimages.com.au/detail/photo/mother-reading-a-book-to-her-two-sons-royalty-free-image/1290705651?phrase=home%20light&searchscope=image%2Cfilm&slot=66)

Many Australian homes were not built to [cope with](https://theconversation.com/australian-homes-can-be-made-climate-ready-reducing-bills-and-emissions-a-new-report-shows-how-219113) a rapidly changing climate.

Compared to new homes, [established houses](https://theconversation.com/living-in-a-glorified-tent-new-research-shows-huge-energy-gaps-between-older-and-newer-homes-286651) tend to consume – and waste – significant amounts of energy.

That’s where home energy upgrade programs come in. These programs help households boost the [energy efficiency](https://theconversation.com/budgets-energy-bill-relief-and-home-retrofit-funding-is-a-good-start-but-dwarfed-by-the-scale-of-the-task-205380) of their houses while cutting power costs, emissions and grid demand. They are mainly run by state and federal governments, but [community-led programs](https://theconversation.com/how-one-local-council-helped-1-200-low-income-residents-finance-solar-and-home-energy-upgrades-278078) are multiplying across Australia.

However, our [recent research](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.erss.2026.104932) shows not all Australians can currently benefit from these programs. Let’s unpack why.

## Top down or bottom up

In Australia, home energy upgrade programs are largely [developed and delivered](https://www.energy.gov.au/rebates) by state, territory and federal governments. These programs assume that if households are given the right information and a financial incentive, they will decide to upgrade. This approach allows them to reach large numbers of people, with Victoria’s scheme alone delivering more than [180,000 upgrades](https://www.esc.vic.gov.au/victorian-energy-upgrades/updates-reports-reviews-and-data/victorian-energy-upgrades-reporting) to households in 2025.

However, government-run programs tend to benefit households that [can pay](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.erss.2026.104589) the residual cost of upgrades, are motivated to change and have the skills to navigate any practical or legal hurdles. This is because energy upgrades can be [costly and complex](https://online.fliphtml5.com/jczqfe/etme/#p=1) to install.

[Community-led programs](https://theconversation.com/no-home-left-behind-a-postcode-approach-to-electrification-241471) are gaining traction in Australia. These programs – run by either communities or [local government](https://theconversation.com/how-one-local-council-helped-1-200-low-income-residents-finance-solar-and-home-energy-upgrades-278078) – are often much more attuned to what residents want and worry about. They are built on trust and relationships, and provide practical advice and hands-on support. These are often what so-called “[hard-to-reach](https://energyconsumersaustralia.com.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/website-doc-consumer-energy-report-card-jun25-report-understanding-measuring-energy-hardship-australia.pdf)” households – such as renters, low-income Australians and people from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds – need most. Without such supports, these households tend to [miss out](https://theconversation.com/like-solar-most-of-the-first-home-battery-subsidies-went-to-the-wealthy-we-need-a-fairer-approach-282495).

One organiser told us:

> “Developing a trustworthy relationship with the household is just key. Otherwise, you get very low uptake of these programs.”

---

***Read more:
[No home left behind: a postcode approach to electrification](https://theconversation.com/no-home-left-behind-a-postcode-approach-to-electrification-241471)***

---

## All about connection

Upgrading a house can involve making lots of [complex decisions](https://theconversation.com/these-5-roadblocks-are-standing-in-the-way-of-energy-efficient-homes-256906). Many local home energy upgrade programs are resource-poor and may have to rely on state or federal schemes, which are [often difficult](https://theconversation.com/these-5-roadblocks-are-standing-in-the-way-of-energy-efficient-homes-256906) to navigate and apply for. This is particularly true for people whose first language is not English or who lack computer skills.

Research consistently shows [trusted relationships](https://doi.org/10.1177/00380385241298177) make upgrading much smoother. They are also key to ensuring locally-led home energy upgrade programs actually work.

To cultivate such relationships, program managers must create opportunities for householders to interact with each other. This could be community forums, appliance demonstration events or open home days where people explain how they upgraded their home and what the results were.

We [interviewed](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.erss.2026.104932) 19 people who design and deliver these programs, working in state government, local government, community groups, peak bodies and consultancies. Most were based in Victoria, with participants also in New South Wales and Queensland, and several working nationally.

A common theme was the value of “social work” in the delivery of home energy upgrade programs. Examples of social work include helping people identify which incentives they are eligible for or guiding them through the application process. Householders may also need help picking the right upgrade products for their home and finding tradies who can safely and effectively install them.

One organiser acknowledged:

> “I really had to hold people’s hand through a lot of it, which is fine if you’re expecting that.”

Another organiser shared:

> “The solar installer that we had, they obviously don’t work with a lot of low-income people because they can’t afford the solar. They weren’t used to working with that type of audience with all of these extra layers of needs.”

---

***Read more:
[Complicated, costly and downright frustrating: Aussies keen to cut emissions with clean energy at home get little support](https://theconversation.com/complicated-costly-and-downright-frustrating-aussies-keen-to-cut-emissions-with-clean-energy-at-home-get-little-support-161682)***

---

## Scaling up

One issue is many locally-led home energy upgrade programs don’t have the funding or resources to last. But we can change that by:

* recognising councils and community organisations as delivery partners in their own right, with a clear role in designing programs and funding that covers dedicated staff
* offering more predictable, [sustainable funding](https://theconversation.com/how-one-local-council-helped-1-200-low-income-residents-finance-solar-and-home-energy-upgrades-278078) to give program managers the time to establish relationships with householders and build on long-term projects
* rethinking how we [measure success](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.erss.2024.103863), by evaluating whether programs build trusted relationships and not just the number of upgrades installed or rebates claimed
* creating ways to share knowledge between local programs by [supporting initiatives](https://www.racefor2030.com.au/project/energy-upgrades-for-australian-homes/) that connect councils and community groups.

Locally-led home energy upgrade programs are [popping up](https://theconversation.com/how-one-local-council-helped-1-200-low-income-residents-finance-solar-and-home-energy-upgrades-278078) across the country. Our research team is [building a platform](https://homeenergyupgrades.com.au/) to give organisers the tools and guidance they need. But to ensure these programs reach all Australian homes, we must recognise and fund them as a critical part of our nation’s [clean energy transition](https://theconversation.com/tracking-the-transition-the-forgotten-emissions-undoing-the-work-of-australias-renewable-energy-boom-162506).

---

***Read more:
[‘Balcony solar’ and plug-in systems could help cut your energy costs. But only if rules change](https://theconversation.com/balcony-solar-and-plug-in-systems-could-help-cut-your-energy-costs-but-only-if-rules-change-285149)***

---

![The Conversation](https://counter.theconversation.com/content/289144/count.gif)

*Christoph Brodnik receives funding for this research as part of the Energy Upgrades for Australian Homes project, which is led by Monash University and funded through the RACE for 2030 Cooperative Research Centre.*

entries.title: Whistleblower: USPSs new ballot screening system isnt ready
entries.content:
![A voter deposits a ballot in a collection box to cast her vote](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/01k2aNhmzw51KDIsX3dVzHd/hero-image.jpg)

A whistleblower working inside the United States Postal Service (USPS) has told Congress that a brand-new system for screening mail-in ballots — built in a matter of months, against the advice of the agency's own staff — is so rushed and untested that it risks mass rejection of legitimate ballots just as the 2026 midterms approach.

The allegations are laid out [in an anonymous disclosure](https://www.blumenthal.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/2026-08-31_final_letter-disclosure.pdf) filed on Aug. 30 with the office of Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-Connecticut) through the nonprofit legal group Whistleblower Aid. The whistleblower, described as a federal official with direct knowledge of the project, says USPS leadership pushed for a Sept. 1 launch despite internal warnings that the software hadn't been properly built or tested, and that development continued at points even while federal courts had ordered the work to stop. Blumenthal's letter demands USPS turn over records and answer detailed questions about the system by early September.

The launch of the new portal is partly in response to [a Trump executive order](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2026/03/ensuring-citizenship-verification-and-integrity-in-federal-elections/) from March 31 directing USPS to write new rules governing how mail-in and absentee ballots move through the postal system. Trump has been adamant the 2020 election was stolen from him, [even as recently as last month](https://www.npr.org/2026/08/19/nx-s1-5938799/trump-census-bureau-noncitizen-voting), as he cited a dubious Census Bureau report to back up his "election fraud" claims.

[A 2025 Brookings analysis](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/mail-voting-in-the-us-data-points-to-very-low-fraud-and-significant-benefits-to-voters/) found that mail-in voter fraud was "very rare," according to their findings. [An additional analysis by American Immigration Council](https://www.americanimmigrationcouncil.org/blog/myths-about-noncitizen-voting-heritage-foundation-data/) also concluded that the Heritage Foundation's report on noncitizen voting proved there "is no crisis of noncitizen voting" and that it's "exceedingly rare."

The White House's purported aim is to verify that only eligible, registered voters receive ballots by mail, using unique barcodes tied to state-maintained voter lists. The EO also adds that states that do not comply could lose federal funding. The U.S. Constitution mandates that [election laws are under state supervision](https://constitution.congress.gov/browse/essay/artI-S4-C1-2/ALDE_00013577/), which includes the tabulation and tracking of mail-in ballots.

USPS published a proposed rule in June and a final rule on Aug. 26 that, for the first time, gives the Postal Service a gatekeeping role over ballot mail — meaning USPS can now refuse to mail ballot batches that state election officials have already prepared and approved. According to Blumenthal's letter, USPS has never previously had this kind of authority over how states run their own ballot mail.

USPS has not yet responded publicly to the specific whistleblower allegations. Here's what the new system is supposed to do, and why the disclosure says it might not work.

## How the new system is supposed to work

To carry this out, USPS has been building an entirely new piece of software called the Federal Ballot Mail Portal. Per the disclosure, the process has three parts:

1. **The Portal itself**, where state election officials upload a list of every registered voter getting a mail ballot, along with each ballot's unique barcode, creating a statewide "Mail-In and Absentee Participation List."
2. **A manifest check**, where officials separately upload a batch manifest. This is basically an inventory of the specific ballots they're about to mail into an older USPS bulk-mail system. USPS then automatically checks whether the barcodes in that manifest match the ones already logged in the Portal.
3. **A physical scan at the post office**, where USPS employees scan a sample of the actual ballots in a batch to confirm the physical barcodes match what's on file, before agreeing to mail the batch at all.

What's causing the most alarm from lawmakers and critics is that if either check fails, USPS won't mail the ballots.

The whistleblower says USPS is enforcing what amounts to a zero-tolerance policy. If even a single ballot's barcode in a batch fails to match or scan properly, the entire batch gets bounced back to the state, the whistleblower alleges.

In action, as the whistleblower describes it, if a state were to bring 10,000 ballots to USPS and just one can't be verified either cause a voter recently changed their name or moved, USPS would decline to mail the other 9,999 as well. States would then have to pull the whole batch, fix the one ballot, and resubmit the entire manifest to restart the verification process from scratch.

Barcode scanning errors aren't hypothetical, either. The disclosure cites a 2017 audit by the USPS Office of Inspector General that looked at problems with package-tracking scanners; among its findings, one unspecified issue was tied to roughly one in 20 scans coming back wrong. Apply even a fraction of that error rate to ballot batches instead of packages, and a meaningful number of valid ballots could get swept up in a rejected batch.

There's also no clear appeals process. The final rule says voters or election officials will be told about "escalation procedures" if they want to challenge a rejection, but doesn't specify what those procedures actually are — and voters may not find out their ballot was part of a rejected batch until it's too late to get another one or vote in person.

## How this affects the 2026 Midterms

According to the disclosure, USPS didn't start serious work on the Portal until around mid-June 2026 and was targeting a Sept. 1 launch. The whistleblower says a project of this complexity would normally take nine months to a year, and cites a member of the Postal Regulatory Commission making a similar estimate publicly.

When staff raised concerns about the compressed schedule, one senior official is said to have brushed them off, insisting the launch simply had to go perfectly with no room for error. Additionally, a federal court order blocked the ballot-mail provisions of the executive order on June 25, but the whistleblower alleges that the order was ignored, and work started up again in the days following the ruling.

By the whistleblower's account, the complete system wasn't even assembled in a testing environment until the week of Aug. 24 — leaving roughly four working days for customer-facing testing before the planned launch, on a system meant to help run a federal election. Sen. Blumenthal has given USPS until Sept. 4 to answer a list of questions, specifically whether USPS actually paused work as required, who authorized development to continue, and whether any testing has been done to catch false rejections. The senator also gave a Sept. 8 deadline to hand over internal records.

Altogether, the USPS mail portal is one of many avenues the White House is pursuing to change the rules governing mail voting before November's midterms. On Aug. 24, the Supreme Court's conservative majority [let the administration move forward](https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/08/supreme-court-allows-trump-administration-to-move-forward-with-order-imposing-restrictions-on-ma/) on the executive order. The majority didn't rule on whether the order was legal — it said the challenge was premature because the rules hadn't been finalized yet, reasoning states couldn't show they'd actually been harmed.

On Capitol Hill, Senate Republicans tried and failed in early August to push through a pared-down version of the [SAVE America Act](https://www.npr.org/2026/06/04/nx-s1-5751145/save-act-senate-vote-trump) requiring photo ID at the polls, after leadership concluded they didn't have the votes for the full bill, which would also mandate proof of citizenship to register and roll back mail voting more broadly. That measure has now failed at least six times this year, but GOP leaders say they'll try again when the Senate reconvenes in this month.

Through these various legal levers, the administration has several routes still open to reshape how — and whether — millions of mail ballots get counted this fall, even without a single bill becoming law.
